title: The Man Who Fell on the Subway
text:
Laboratory studies of the 1960s suggested that people in groups often fail to help in emergencies. In 1968 Irving Piliavin, Judith Rodin and Jane Piliavin tested this in a real and crowded setting: the New York subway.

Teams of students rode an express train in Manhattan on a stretch with no stops for about seven and a half minutes. Shortly after the train left the station, a young man staggered forward and collapsed on the floor, then lay staring up at the ceiling. In some trials he carried a cane and seemed sober and ill. In others he smelled of liquor and carried a bottle wrapped in a paper bag, looking drunk. Observers quietly recorded what the passengers did.

The man with the cane received help nearly every time, usually within seconds and before any planted helper could step in. The apparently drunk man was helped less often and more slowly, though still in about half the trials. Unlike in the laboratory, larger numbers of passengers did not slow helping down. On the subway the need was obvious and no one could leave the car, and in those conditions ordinary New Yorkers acted quickly. When help did come, men were much more likely than women to give it.
lesson: People help readily when the need is clear and they cannot drift away. When you need help, make the need plain and direct, and when you see it, do not wait for others.
people: Irving Piliavin, Judith Rodin, Jane Piliavin
location: New York City subway, New York, USA
source: Piliavin, I. M., Rodin, J., and Piliavin, J. A. (1969). Good Samaritanism: An underground phenomenon? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 13(4), 289-299.
